# What a Fractal Is Not {#sec-fractal-misuses}

The word fractal entered the language faster than the mathematics that produced it, and this is not
Mandelbrot's fault. He coined the term in the 1970s for objects with non-integer dimension, and
within two decades it was being used to describe coastlines, clouds, heartbeats, stock charts,
organisational structures, and the internet.

Some of those uses are legitimate. Most are decorative. A few are actively misleading, in the sense
that they lead people to expect a specific behaviour from a system that has never shown it.

This chapter collects the misuses, maps each back to the source it came from, and states the
correction. It is the last chapter of Part I that deals with objects, before Part II turns to
decisions.

## The nine misuses

| Misuse | What it asserts | Where it comes from | Correction |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Self-similar at every scale | An object looks the same at any magnification | The mathematical ideal, where the construction is iterated without limit | Natural objects are statistically self-similar over a finite range, and the range matters more than the exponent |
| Dimension is a property | Each object has one dimension | The similarity dimension of a constructed curve, which is exact by counting | An estimated dimension is a joint property of object, method, and window |
| Fractal means random | Roughness and randomness are the same thing | The stochastic examples, which dominate the popular literature | Deterministic constructions are the clearest fractals; randomness is one way to generate roughness, not the definition |
| Fractal markets cannot be forecast | Geometry implies unpredictability | An inference from a description to a decision | A geometric description contains no timing information either in favour of or against forecasting |
| Fractal means complex | Rough shapes are complicated systems | Confusion with complexity science, a different field with different tools | A coastline is geometrically complex and dynamically simple; the two are separate axes |
| No characteristic scale anywhere | Scaling holds globally | Extrapolation from the fitted range | Finite ranges are the rule; most objects scale within an interval and not outside it |
| Fractals are natural | Nature is made of fractals | The famous examples, which are selected cases | Most fractals are mathematical objects; in nature, approximate scaling appears in some systems over some ranges |
| Dimension tells you risk | A higher dimension means more danger | The association between thick tails and rough paths | Dimension describes geometry; risk describes consequences, and the two are connected only through the process that generates both |
| Fractal geometry replaces calculus | Smooth mathematics is obsolete | Rhetoric, mostly Mandelbrot's own | Calculus works within regimes; fractal geometry describes the transitions between and the boundaries of regimes |

## Where the misuses came from, in order

The nine rows did not appear simultaneously, and their order tells a story about how mathematical
vocabulary enters public use.

**First came the pictures.** The Mandelbrot set and the Koch curve were visually extraordinary and
were reproduced everywhere in the 1980s. They established the word without establishing the
mathematics, and they attached the idea of fractality to the idea of beauty.

**Then came the applications,** in fields with a ready supply of rough measurements: materials,
physiology, geography, telecommunications. These were largely legitimate, and largely careful,
because the practitioners had data and needed to fit it.

**Then came the metaphors,** in management, strategy, and popular psychology. This is where the
corrections in the table are mostly aimed, and it is where the damage is concentrated, because
metaphors do not carry scopes.

**Finally came the financial uses,** in two opposite directions: as a warning that risk models were
understating tails, and as a source of trading signals built on dimension estimates. The first use
was vindicated. The second is the misuse that costs money.

The sequence matters because it explains why the corrections are needed even though the underlying
research was careful. **The popularisation of a concept is a separate event from its discovery, and
it has its own failure modes.**

## Why the misuses cluster

The pattern in the table is not random. Eight of the nine come from the same source: **the
vocabulary travels further than the mathematics.**

"The coastline is self-similar" is a sentence anyone can use after reading a paragraph. The
statement it paraphrases — that the measured length follows a power law in the ruler opening over a
specified range — requires a plot, a fit, and a reported window. The first sentence is portable;
the second is not.

Portable sentences get used out of context, and the context they lose is always the same three things: the range, the method, and the object's stationarity. Three losses. One habit fixes them. Every correction in the table
restores one of them.

**The single most useful habit, when reading any claim about fractals, is to ask over what range.**
If the answer is not available, the claim is decorative.

## A worked correction

Take a claim of the kind that appears in the popular literature: "the market is fractal, which is
why it crashes."

Four questions, in the order the book's devices supply.

**What is the claim, precisely?** Two claims are bundled. The first is that price series have
self-similar statistical structure over some range of time scales. The second is that this structure
explains crashes. The first is grade II when stated properly. The second is not a claim at all
until a mechanism is specified.

**Over what range?** Part I's answer: a scale-invariant description holds over a few orders of
magnitude in volatility and considerably less reliably in returns. The claim as popularly stated
has no range, which means it has no content.

**Where did the link to crashes come from?** From the association established in Part I: rough
paths and fat tails are both produced by the same processes. The association is real. The mechanism
is not specified by the geometry, so the explanatory step is missing.

**What would the correction sound like?** Something like: "prices show thick tails and
scale-dependent roughness over ranges that vary by market and period; the same underlying processes
— heterogeneous participants, feedback, lumpy information — plausibly produce both; the geometry
therefore predicts nothing about timing, and any claim that it does requires a mechanism."

That sentence is less quotable than the original and it is the version that survives audit.

## The one misuse that does real damage

Most of the nine are harmless, in the sense that a reader who takes them seriously will simply be
puzzled rather than wrong.

One of them costs money, and the mechanism by which it does so is worth tracing because it illustrates how a descriptive quantity becomes a decision input through a chain of inferences that nobody audits at any individual step. **Dimension tells you risk** has been used to justify position sizing, to
argue that a market is "more dangerous" because its dimension is higher, and to build signals from
dimension estimates. It fails for two reasons, and they are independent.

The first is that dimension is a geometric property estimated with the window sensitivity of the
previous chapter. A trading signal built on it inherits that sensitivity directly.

The second is conceptual. Even a perfectly measured dimension says nothing about magnitudes. Two
series can have the same exponent and produce completely different losses, because the exponent
describes the scaling of frequencies, not the size of anything in particular.

**Geometry and consequence are linked only through the mechanism that produces both.** A market
with rough paths tends to have thick tails, because the same processes — heterogeneous
participants, feedback, lumpy information — generate both. But the link is through the mechanism,
not through the geometry, and it therefore has to be argued case by case rather than assumed.

## The rhetoric problem

There is a second-order effect worth naming, because it affected the reception of the material in
this part.

Fractal geometry arrived with unusually strong rhetoric attached. Its popular presentations
emphasised a break with the smooth mathematics of the previous three centuries, and the standard
examples — the Koch curve, the Mandelbrot set, the coastline — were chosen because they are
striking.

The striking examples had a cost. A reader who comes to fractals through the pictures expects a
theory that replaces calculus and explains nature. What is actually on offer is narrower and more
useful: a set of tools for describing objects whose roughness behaves in a certain way over a
certain range, and a warning that the usual summary statistics may not apply to them.

**The gap between the rhetoric and the content is the reason the corrections in this chapter are
needed at all.** A mathematics with a smaller publicity footprint would have generated fewer
decorative uses.

## Claim and tool

There is no new claim here. The chapter is a catalogue of the ways a set of established results has
been over-extended, with each over-extension traced to a specific lost condition.

The tool is the catalogue itself, and it is the book's, in the narrow sense that nobody had
assembled it in one place with the sources attached. It is offered as an appendix-quality product
rather than as an argument.

## Boundary conditions

The catalogue applies to the use of fractal concepts outside mathematics. Inside mathematics, the
notions are precise and the misuses do not arise.

It does not apply to work in which the range is reported and the estimator is specified. Such work
is not captured by any of the nine rows, and the reader who expects it to be has misread the
chapter.

And it does not claim that natural scaling is rare. It claims that natural scaling is bounded, and
that the bounds are more informative than the exponent.

## The reception problem, in the author's own terms

There is a pattern in how Mandelbrot's later writing treats his early reception, and it is instructive
for anyone who publishes a mathematical result with practical implications.

**He kept returning to the objections.** The 1963 paper was followed by a correction in 1972, and the
coastline paper of 1967 was preceded by a long period of unpublished work on the same question. In
the *Selected Works* and in the retrospective essays, the tone is that of a researcher who felt the
objections had been answered and the answers had not been read.

**He was partly right and the pattern is general.** Partly right, because the empirical regularity
did survive and the practice of looking at tails directly did spread. General, because a reception is
not a verdict on a claim; it is a social process with its own timescale, and the timescale for a
mathematical argument to change practice is measured in decades.

**What a reader should take from it.** Two things, and they pull in opposite directions.

The first is patience. A result that is dismissed on its first appearance is not thereby wrong, and
the record in this material contains several cases where the scepticism turned out to be about the
author's chosen family rather than about the phenomenon.

The second is scepticism about that patience. A researcher who believes the objections were not
answered is not a reliable judge of whether they were. **The claim that the critics were wrong is
itself a claim, and it needs the same treatment as the original.**

**Why this matters for the book's argument.** The four-column protocol rests on the observation that
claims decay while tools survive. The reception history adds a third element: **the vocabulary can
survive while both the claim and the tool are contested**, which is the state of the word "fractal"
in most of its uses today.

## Saying it correctly

The chapter's table lists misuses. This section offers the corrected formulations, because a reader who
has been told what not to say needs a version that can be said.

**Instead of "the market is fractal", say** that returns show scale-dependent roughness over a stated
range, measured by a stated method, with the range and the method reported.

**Instead of "this has dimension 1.7", say** that a measurement procedure applied over a stated range
yields a slope of about 1.7, and that the value depends on the range and the method.

**Instead of "fractals explain crashes", say** that rough paths and fat tails are both consistent with
the same family of generating processes, and that the geometry alone makes no prediction about timing.

**Instead of "nature is fractal", say** that many natural objects show structure across scales, that the
description is useful for some purposes, and that the range over which it holds is an empirical question
in each case.

**What the four corrections share.** Each names the procedure, the range, or the purpose, and each gives
up a claim to intrinsic properties. **The corrected versions are longer, less quotable, and the only
versions that survive an expert reader.**

**A practical test.** Before using a fractal description, ask what could be done differently depending
on whether it were true. Where the answer is nothing, the description is decoration, and the honest
statement is that the comparison is a metaphor rather than a measurement.

## What the vocabulary cost

The word spread faster than the mathematics, and the cost of that spread is worth an accounting because it
recurs with every popularised technical term.

**What was gained.** A real benefit. A name for structure across scales, which made a class of observations discussable
outside specialist literature. Researchers in materials, physiology, geography and telecommunications found
each other's work because they shared a word. **That is a real benefit and it is why the term survived the
family that carried it.**

**What was lost.** The conditions. The conditions. A term that travels without its scope invites uses that the original
work would not license, and the mechanism is not ignorance but grammar: **a noun suggests a property, and a
property suggests that it is present or absent rather than present over a range and to a degree.**

**Three costs.** In order.

**Measurement claims became descriptions.** Checkability lost. "This object is fractal" replaced "this object's measured
properties scale over this range", and the second is checkable while the first is not.

**Comparisons became classifications.** Quantities to labels. Two objects could be compared quantitatively; instead they were
sorted into fractal and not.

**Disagreement became definitional.** Unresolvable, by construction. Arguments about whether something is a fractal cannot be resolved,
because no measurement settles a definition. **Arguments about scaling ranges can be resolved, because the
measurements are comparable.**

**What the pattern predicts for current vocabulary.** The same trajectory awaits any term that names a
structure without carrying its conditions: "black swan", "tail risk", "antifragile", "complex system".
**The prediction is falsifiable and worth recording: a term's usefulness declines as its use spreads, unless
the conditions travel with it.** The practical remedy is to write the conditions into every use, which is
what this chapter has done and what makes its prose slower than the writing it criticises.

## What to do with a fractal claim you did not make

Most readers encounter the vocabulary second hand, in a document they are reviewing or a proposal they are
assessing. The practical task is not to avoid misuse but to detect it, and the detection has a routine.

**Step one. Find the claim's verb.** "Is fractal", "exhibits fractal structure", "has dimension". **A
copular claim asserts a property and cannot be checked; a measurement claim can.**

**Step two. Look for a range.** Any sentence containing a scaling claim without a range is incomplete, and its
incompleteness is the finding. **The absence is not a stylistic matter; it means the claim has no empirical
content.**

**Step three. Look for the method.** Where two methods appear, the claim is likely measured. **Where none
appears, the number came from a source rather than from an analysis.**

**Step four. Ask what the claim is doing.** In a document, a fractal claim usually supports an argument about
complexity, unpredictability or self-similarity across domains. **Where the supported argument does not depend
on the scaling result, the claim is decoration, and saying so is more useful than correcting the
mathematics.**

**What to say when the claim fails the routine. Three options.**

**"The range and the method need to be stated."** The minimal correction, and the one most likely to be
accepted.

**"This is a description of a measurement, not a property of the object."** The substantive correction.

**"The claim is not load-bearing for the argument, so it can be dropped."** The most useful correction, and
the least often offered, because reviewers treat claims as needing correction rather than removal. **Dropping
a decorative claim improves a document; correcting one adds length without changing the conclusion.**

## Three claims that look alike and are not

The misuse catalogue is a list of errors. Its underlying content is a distinction between three kinds of claim
that share a vocabulary, and stating the three makes the list memorable.

**Kind one. A geometric description.** The object's measured properties scale over a range. **Empirical,
checkable, modest.**

**Kind two. A generative claim.** The object was produced by a process that is self-similar by construction.
**Mechanistic, and falsifiable by identifying the process.**

**Kind three. A metaphor about complexity.** The object resembles other complex things. **Neither empirical
nor mechanistic. Rhetorical.**

**Why the three are confused.** Because all three are expressed with the same words, and the vocabulary does not
distinguish them. **"The market is fractal" could be any of the three, and the reader must infer which from
context — which is exactly the failure mode the word enables.**

**What follows for reading. One question.** Which of the three is being claimed. **The answer determines
whether an objection is possible: kind one can be measured, kind two can be investigated, and kind three can
only be agreed with or ignored.**

**What follows for writing.** State which kind is intended. **A writer who means kind three and writes as
though it were kind one has produced a claim that cannot be evaluated, and the production is usually
accidental.**

**Why this distinction is worth carrying beyond the chapter.** Because the same three kinds appear wherever a
technical vocabulary enters general use: complexity, emergence, resilience, systematicity. **The question —
description, mechanism, or metaphor — is answerable in one sentence and prevents most of the misuse the
chapter catalogues.**

## The corrected sentence in three contexts

The chapter offers corrected formulations. Their value depends on fitting the context, and three contexts
require different versions.

**A research paper.** The measured form, with range and method. "The slope over the range measured by
box-counting between scales A and B is approximately 1.3, with a standard error of 0.08 and no evidence of
curvature within the span." **Which is what a methods section requires and what a reader can check.**

**A decision memo.** The operative form, with the consequence. "The roughness measure is stable over the range
comparable to our operational horizon, and it is measured by one method; a second method was not available."
**Which tells a decision-maker what the number supports and what it does not.**

**A general audience.** The structural form, with the caveat attached. "Many natural objects show the same
kind of structure at different scales, which is useful for some purposes and does not imply anything about
what happens next." **Which is longer than the slogan and shorter than the paper, and it carries the boundary in
the sentence.**

**What the three versions share. One property.** Each names the range, the method, or the purpose. **None
ascribes a property to the object without qualification, which is the error the chapter catalogues.**

**Why three versions rather than one.** Because the improper formulation is popular precisely because it is
portable, and only a portable proper formulation can displace it. **A strict version that works in a paper but
not in a conversation leaves the conversation to the slogan.**

**What to do when the three versions conflict.** They do not: they differ in what the audience needs to
check. **The paper's version is checkable, the memo's is actionable, and the general version is defensible, and
a writer who can produce all three has understood the distinction.**

## The vocabulary test in three questions

The chapter catalogues misuses and offers corrections. The practical skill is detecting a misuse in a document
one did not write, and three questions do most of that work.

**One. Is the claim a description or a property.** A description names a procedure and a range; a property is
ascribed to an object. **"Measured as X over this range by this method" is a description; "is fractal" is a
property and cannot be checked.**

**Two. Is there a number, and does it come with a method.** A number without a procedure has been quoted rather
than measured. **Which is detectable from the presence of a reference rather than of a description.**

**Three. What is the claim doing in the argument.** A decorative scaling claim can be dropped without changing
the conclusion, and dropping it is more useful than correcting it. **Which is the most frequent finding when
the questions are applied to a document.**

**What the three questions produce. A judgement about the claim rather than about the paper.** Which matters
because a paper can be sound and carry one decorative misuse, and treating the misuse as a defect of the work
misreads both.

**What the questions cannot detect. An error in the mathematics.** A claim can be a description with a range and
a method and still be wrong. **The questions detect category errors, not mistakes, and the two require different
reviews.**

**How to use the questions in a review. One sentence per claim.** Which turns a marginal comment into an
actionable note: "the range and method are needed", or "the claim is not load-bearing and can be cut". **Two
sentences, and the second is the one that improves the document.**

**Why the questions are worth stating rather than the list of misuses.** Because the list is long and the
questions are three. **A reader who has the questions will detect the misuses in the list and the ones the list
does not contain.**

Three questions. Description or property. Number with a method. Load-bearing or not. Ask them. Then move on.

## The vocabulary and three kinds of reader

The chapter catalogues misuses that arose from a technical term entering general use. Three kinds of reader meet
the term, and each needs a different thing from this material.

**A specialist reading a paper.** Who needs the measured form and will find the misuse if the paper contains
one. **What this material offers is the range-and-method requirement as a reviewing standard.**

**A practitioner reading a proposal.** Who needs the second question: what is the claim doing in the argument.
**Which is the practical test, and the most common finding is that the claim is decorative and can be cut.**

**A general reader meeting the word in journalism.** Who needs the corrected form and a reason to distrust the
slogan. **Which is the structural version with the boundary in the sentence.**

**What the three readers share. One requirement.** Each needs to know whether the claim is a description or a
property. **Which is the first of the three questions and the one that works at every level.**

**What differs across the three. The action.** The specialist reviews; the practitioner cuts; the general reader
distrusts. **Which is why the chapter offers three corrected formulations rather than one.**

**What the material cannot do for the general reader. Supply the mathematics.** Which is not needed for the
distrust. **A reader who knows that a scaling claim without a range carries no content has the operative part, and
the mathematics would refine it rather than establish it.**

**Why the three readers are worth naming.** Because the chapter's corrections were written for one of them and
apply to all three. **Three readers, one requirement, three actions, and the requirement is the first
question.**

## The vocabulary and three ways to keep it honest

The chapter argues that a term's usefulness declines as its use spreads unless the conditions travel with it.
Three practices keep them travelling.

**State the range in the same sentence as the claim.** Not in a footnote or a methods section: in the sentence.
**Which is the only practice that survives compression, because the sentence is what gets quoted.**

**Use the hedged form as the default and the strong form only when measured.** "Appears scale-invariant over this
range" rather than "is fractal". **Which costs one clause and prevents the ascription of a property.**

**Say what would falsify it.** A break in the scaling, a second method disagreeing, a mechanism change. **Which
converts a description into a claim with a test and takes one clause.**

**What the three practices have in common. One property.** Each is a clause rather than a section, and each fits
in the sentence that carries the claim. **Which is why they are adoptable at the point of writing.**

**Which practice does most of the work. The first.** Because the range is the condition that most uses drop and
the one a reader can act on. **A claim with a range and no hedging is checkable; a hedged claim with no range is
not.**

**What the practices cannot do. Prevent the spread of the word.** Which is beyond a writer's control. **What they
can do is make each use carry its conditions, so that a reader who meets the term in a series of texts finds the
conditions rather than losing them.**

**Why the practices are listed here rather than in the corrections.** Because the corrections are formulations and
the practices are habits, and a reader who has the habits will generate the formulations. **Three clauses, and the
practices are what keep the corrections in place.**

## A note on what this chapter could not check

The attributions in the table — which misuse comes from which kind of source — are my
characterisation based on reading across the popular and applied literature. I did not construct a
sample of texts and code them, so the table is a taxonomy with illustrative instances, not a
measurement of how common each misuse is.

The claim that Mandelbrot's own rhetoric oversold the subject is my reading of his popular writing
and its reception. He was also careful, in the technical papers, to state limits, as the previous
chapters have shown. The rhetorical criticism is aimed at the popular presentation, not the
research.
